title: PostgreSQL With Raw SQL
summary: See what an ORM does and why this course skips it, then connect with JdbcClient, run migrations, and write safe parameterized queries.
intro: Roombook's repository still keeps its bookings in memory, and the previous lesson designed the tables that will replace it. This lesson connects the two. It starts with a choice every project makes: most frameworks offer an ORM, a library that writes your SQL for you, and this course writes its own SQL with Spring's `JdbcClient` over PgJDBC instead, for reasons part 1 explains. Then it opens a pool of database connections, creates the tables with migrations, reads rows without letting anyone inject SQL, writes rows, and turns the database's errors into API errors. By the end, the in-memory repository is gone, and the service never noticed.

steps.title: ORMs, and why this course writes SQL
steps.body:
Every Spring Boot project decides how its code talks to the database, and the choice shapes the rest of the code. The popular answer is an ORM. This course takes the other road and writes its SQL by hand. This part explains what an ORM does, what it costs, and why learning SQL first is the better start.

## What an ORM does

An **ORM**, an object-relational mapper, maps your classes to tables and your objects to rows. You describe a Booking class once, and the ORM writes the SQL. Saving a new object becomes an INSERT, changing a field and saving becomes an UPDATE, and a call like `bookingRepository.findByUserId(userId)`, from Spring Data JPA, which generates the query from the method's name, becomes a SELECT. Many ORMs also create the tables from your classes.

That's appealing. Simple endpoints need very little code, the types come for free, and you rarely write SQL at all.

## What it costs

- **You can't see the queries.** The SQL is made at run time, out of sight. A harmless-looking line can send a query that reads a whole table, and you find out when the endpoint is slow.
- **The N+1 problem.** You met N+1 with GraphQL's resolvers, and ORMs cause it the same way. Most load related rows lazily, the first time your code touches them. List 50 bookings and show each one's room name, and the ORM sends one query for the bookings, then one more for each booking's room: 51 queries where one JOIN would do. It's the most common reason ORM code is slow.
- **It's a second language.** Each ORM has its own way to write filters, joins, and groups, and whatever it can't express falls back to SQL. So you end up needing both.
- **It hides what the database can do.** The rules that keep Roombook correct, like refusing two bookings that overlap, are database features most ORMs can't describe. Teams on an ORM often skip them, and the rule moves into code that a second writer can get around.

## The spectrum

Database libraries fall along a line, from writing every query yourself to never seeing one:

```diagram raw-sql-spectrum
From writing every query yourself to never seeing one.
```

- A **driver** sends the SQL you write and hands back the rows. This course uses Spring's `JdbcClient` over PgJDBC.
- A **query builder** builds SQL from function calls, which helps when a query changes shape at run time.
- **SQL-first** tools read SQL you write in files and give you typed functions that run it.
- An **ORM** maps classes to tables and writes the SQL itself.

| Step | Libraries for Java and Spring |
|---|---|
| Driver | PgJDBC, through JDBC and Spring's `JdbcClient` |
| Query builder | jOOQ, which also generates classes from your tables |
| SQL-first mapping | MyBatis, and Spring Data JDBC as a light mapper |
| ORM | JPA with Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA on top |

JPA, the Jakarta Persistence API, is the ORM standard most Spring tutorials reach for first. This course skips it so the SQL stays in plain sight, and `JdbcClient` keeps the plumbing short.

## Why this course writes SQL

You'll learn what the database really does, and every query Roombook sends sits in its repository, where you can read it, check it with EXPLAIN, and fix it. SQL also lasts. It's the same in every language and framework, so what you learn here carries over to your next project, while an ORM's API doesn't. And picking up an ORM once you know SQL is easy, because you can see through it. Going the other way is hard.

None of that makes ORMs wrong. Plenty of teams ship good software with one, especially apps that are mostly forms over tables. When you meet one, you'll know what it does underneath, and that's when it helps most.

steps.title: Connecting through a pool
steps.body:
Every request that reads or writes data needs a connection to the database, and the way you manage connections decides how many requests the API can serve at once. Opening a new one for each request is the classic first mistake. This part explains what a connection costs, how a pool fixes it, and how Roombook opens one at startup and closes it at shutdown.

## What a connection costs

A connection is a long-lived conversation between your API and the database server. Opening one takes several steps: a TCP connection, often a TLS handshake for encryption, then logging in with a user name and password. PostgreSQL then starts a new process on the server just for that connection, which costs time and several megabytes of memory. Altogether that's a few milliseconds before the first query can run, often longer than the query itself.

The server also limits how many connections it accepts at once, 100 by default, a setting called `max_connections`. An API that opens one per request hits that limit under load, and the requests past it fail.

## A pool

A **connection pool** opens a few connections and keeps them open. When a request needs the database, it **borrows** a connection, runs its queries, and **returns** it, so the next request can use it. Borrowing an open connection takes microseconds.

```diagram raw-sql-pool
Four requests share three open connections. The fourth waits for one to come back.
```

In the diagram, three requests each hold a connection, and the fourth waits. If no connection comes back in time, the pool gives up with a timeout error, which the API answers with a 503. That limit is a feature: it keeps a burst of traffic from flooding the database.

A small pool is usually right. PostgreSQL works on only as many queries at once as its server has CPU cores, so a pool of 100 just moves the queue from your API into the database, where waiting costs more. Ten connections for each copy of the API is a good start. Each copy has its own pool, so the copies times the pool size must stay under `max_connections`. The lesson on databases at scale comes back to that.

## The connection URL

The pool needs to know where the database is and how to log in. That's the connection URL from psql in the previous lesson. It comes from the environment, never from the code, because it holds a password and differs on every computer:

```env
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/roombook
SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=roombook
SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=roombook
```

Java's drivers use their own form of the URL, starting with `jdbc:`, with the user name and password kept apart. Spring Boot reads these three variables by itself, through the relaxed binding from the first project lesson, and uses them in place of the matching settings in `application.yaml`.

## Open at startup, close at shutdown

Spring Boot builds the pool for you. Add the JDBC starter and the PostgreSQL driver to `pom.xml`:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jdbc</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
  <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
  <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
```

Then give it your own computer's database in `src/main/resources/application.yaml`:

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/roombook
    username: roombook
    password: roombook
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      connection-timeout: 5s
```

At startup, Boot creates a **DataSource**, Java's standard name for something that hands out connections. It's backed by **HikariCP**, the pool Spring Boot uses by default. `connection-timeout` is how long a request waits to borrow a connection before it gets an error. Boot also creates a `JdbcClient` bean on top of the pool, which repositories take in their constructor, and it closes the pool when the app stops.

Recall from the first project lesson that Tomcat runs each request on its own thread. A thread that needs the database waits for a free connection. With virtual threads turned on, thousands of requests can be in flight at once, and the pool, not the number of threads, decides how many reach the database. That's the pool doing its job.

steps.title: Migrations in plain SQL
steps.body:
Your tables have to exist before the API can use them, and they'll change as Roombook grows: a new column, a new index, a new table. Every copy of the database, on your computer, on a teammate's, in the tests, and in production, needs exactly the same changes in the same order. Typing CREATE TABLE into psql on each one can't keep up. Migrations do.

## What a migration is

A **migration** is a file of SQL that changes the schema by one step, with a number in its name that sets its place in line. A **migration runner** keeps a table in the database that records which files have run. Each time, it applies the files that aren't in that table yet, in order, each inside a **transaction**, a group of statements that takes effect completely or not at all, and records them. So a fresh database gets every file, and one that's up to date gets none.

PostgreSQL can undo a CREATE TABLE or an ALTER TABLE that fails halfway, which many databases can't. So a migration that fails leaves nothing behind, and you can fix the file and run it again.

## The rules

- **Never edit a migration that has run anywhere but your own computer.** Other databases already applied the old version and won't run it again, so your change would reach some databases and not others. Fix it forward with a new migration.
- **One change per file, named for what it does**: `V4__create_bookings.sql`, `V5__add_bookings_no_overlap.sql`.
- **Keep data out of them, mostly.** Data to try things with, like Ada and the Turing room, goes in a separate seed script. A migration moves data only when the schema change needs it.
- **Make each change safe for the code that's already running.** While a new version rolls out, old copies of the API still run against the new schema. Adding a column is safe. Renaming one breaks the old code, so you add the new column, copy the data, switch the code over, and drop the old column in a later release.

## Roombook's first migrations

Roombook starts with four files, one per table, in the order the foreign keys need them: `V1__create_buildings.sql`, `V2__create_users.sql`, `V3__create_rooms.sql`, and `V4__create_bookings.sql`. Buildings come first, since rooms point at them, and bookings last. Here's `src/main/resources/db/migration/V4__create_bookings.sql`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (START WITH 1001) PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES rooms (id),
  user_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
  starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  ends_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  attendees integer NOT NULL CHECK (attendees > 0),
  note text,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'confirmed'
    CHECK (status IN ('confirmed', 'cancelled')),
  version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  cancelled_at timestamptz,
  CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
);

CREATE INDEX bookings_user_starts_idx ON bookings (user_id, starts_at);
CREATE INDEX bookings_room_starts_idx ON bookings (room_id, starts_at);
```

The other three files hold the CREATE TABLE statements from the data modeling lesson, with the CHECK rules, the foreign keys, and the unique index on `lower(email)` there from the start. The next lesson explains those rules, along with the one against overlapping bookings, which arrives in the fifth migration.

## The runner: Flyway

Spring Boot runs **Flyway** for you when it's on the classpath. Add it next to the JDBC starter:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-flyway</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
  <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

The files go in `src/main/resources/db/migration`, named `V` plus a version, two underscores, and a description, like `V1__create_buildings.sql`. At startup, before the app takes a single request, Flyway compares the files with its table, `flyway_schema_history`, and runs the new ones in order, each in a transaction. It logs each migration it applies, and says when the schema is already up to date.

Flyway also stores a **checksum** of each file, a short fingerprint of its contents. If a file that already ran has changed, Flyway refuses to go on, and the app doesn't start. That's the never-edit rule, enforced for you. The deployment lesson moves migrations into their own release step, so a new version's changes are in place before its first copy starts.

steps.title: Parameters, not string building

examples.title: An injection, and the same input as a parameter
examples.prompt: The first two queries are the ones the string-building code sends. The rest run the same lookup with a real parameter, in psql, using PREPARE, which names a statement with a placeholder, and EXECUTE, which runs it with a value.
examples.output:
id |        email         |  role
----+----------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example | member
(1 row)

 id |         email          |  role
----+------------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example   | member
  2 | grace@roombook.example | staff
  3 | alan@roombook.example  | admin
(3 rows)

PREPARE

 id |        email         |  role
----+----------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example | member
(1 row)

 id | email | role
----+-------+------
(0 rows)
examples.explanation: The first query finds Ada. The second is what the email `' OR '1'='1` turned the code's query into, and it returns all three users, Alan the admin included, without anyone knowing a password. The prepared version takes the same input as a value for `$1`. To write it in SQL, each quote inside the value is doubled, but PostgreSQL then sees one value: the text `' OR '1'='1`. No user has that email, so it finds none. That's exactly what the driver does for you on every query, with no doubling needed, since the values never mix with the text.

examples.title: When a record doesn't fit the row
examples.prompt: Map a room without a RowMapper, with `.query(Room.class)` and a record whose `amenities` is a `List<String>`. The output is the exception it throws.
examples.output: org.springframework.core.convert.ConverterNotFoundException: No converter found capable of converting from type [org.postgresql.jdbc.PgArray] to type [java.util.List<java.lang.String>]
examples.explanation: PgJDBC returns an array column as a `java.sql.Array`, here its own `PgArray`, and Spring has no converter from that to a `List<String>`, so the mapping fails on the first row. The message names both types, which tells you which column to fix. The fix is a RowMapper that reads the array itself: `List.of((String[]) rs.getArray("amenities").getArray())`. An enum stored in lowercase fails too, since `BookingStatus.valueOf("confirmed")` finds no constant. Mapping by name is handy for simple rows, and a RowMapper written out is the reliable choice for anything else.

steps.title: Lists: filters, pages, and N+1

examples.title: Two pages of Ada's bookings
examples.prompt: Ada has five bookings in the seed data, and a page holds two. Ask for three rows to learn whether there's a next page, then ask for the page after the last row shown.
examples.code:
-- Page 1: two bookings, plus one more to learn if a next page exists.
SELECT id, room_id, starts_at
FROM bookings
WHERE user_id = 1
ORDER BY starts_at, id
LIMIT 3;

-- Page 2: the rows after the last one shown, (2026-10-06 10:00, id 1002).
SELECT id, room_id, starts_at
FROM bookings
WHERE user_id = 1
  AND (starts_at, id) > ('2026-10-06 10:00Z', 1002)
ORDER BY starts_at, id
LIMIT 3;
examples.explanation: The first query returns three rows, one more than a page, so there's a next page. The API sends bookings 1001 and 1002, and builds the cursor from booking 1002: its start, 6 October at 10:00, and its id. The second query starts right after that pair and again gets three rows, so it sends 1004 and 1005, and there's a page after it too. Bookings 1005 and 1006 start at exactly the same moment, and only the id decides their order. Without it, the cut between two pages could fall between them and lose one. Booking 1003 never shows up, since it's Grace's. These are the seed script's bookings, so 1002 here starts on 6 October with no note: the 1002 from the request data lesson, with its Chemistry revision note, lived only in memory.

examples.title: Sending an Instant as a parameter
examples.prompt: Pass a `java.time.Instant` straight to a placeholder, without turning it into an `OffsetDateTime`. The output is the cause of the exception Spring throws.
examples.code:
jdbc.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM bookings WHERE starts_at >= :from")
    .param("from", Instant.parse("2026-10-05T00:00:00Z"))
    .query(Long.class)
    .single();
examples.output: org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: Can't infer the SQL type to use for an instance of java.time.Instant. Use setObject() with an explicit Types value to specify the type to use.
examples.explanation: PgJDBC follows JDBC's list of supported Java types, and `Instant` isn't on it, even though it's the type Java programs use most for a moment in time. So the driver can't tell which PostgreSQL type to send, and refuses. Spring wraps that in a `DataAccessException`, and `getMostSpecificCause()` digs out the driver's own message. `OffsetDateTime` is on the list, and maps to `timestamptz` exactly, which is why the repository converts each `Instant` with `atOffset(ZoneOffset.UTC)` before binding it. Reading goes the other way, `getObject(column, OffsetDateTime.class).toInstant()`.

steps.title: Writing rows and reading errors

examples.title: Writing, and getting the result back
examples.prompt: With only the first three seeded bookings, 1001 to 1003, in the table, create a booking, change its attendees and clear its note in one UPDATE, then try to cancel booking 99.
examples.explanation: The INSERT gave the new booking the next id, 1004, and filled `status` and `version` from their defaults, and RETURNING sent them back with no second query. The UPDATE set two columns and bumped `version` to 2. Its note is NULL now, which psql prints as an empty space. The last UPDATE matched nothing, since there's no booking 99, so it reports `UPDATE 0` rather than an error, and the repository's count check is what turns that into a 404. `updated_at = now()` keeps the time of the last change, and the next lesson moves that job into the database.

examples.title: What a broken rule looks like through JdbcClient
examples.prompt: Try to book room 99 and print what Spring throws, with the SQLSTATE and message of the driver's exception underneath.
examples.output:
DataIntegrityViolationException 23503
ERROR: insert or update on table "bookings" violates foreign key constraint "bookings_room_id_fkey"
  Detail: Key (room_id)=(99) is not present in table "rooms".
examples.explanation: Spring threw a `DataIntegrityViolationException`, its exception for a broken rule, and the driver's exception underneath carries the SQLSTATE, `23503`, a foreign key violation. The message names the exact rule, the foreign key PostgreSQL named for `bookings.room_id`, and its `Detail` line says which value broke it. That detail is for your logs, not for the client, since it can include data the caller shouldn't see. In the repository, `translate` reads the SQLSTATE and throws the domain's `room-not-found` problem, a 422.

recap:
- An ORM writes SQL for you and hides it, with N+1 queries as the classic cost, and this course writes SQL with JdbcClient instead.
- A pool keeps a few connections open, each request borrows one, and the pool opens at startup and closes at shutdown.
- Migrations are numbered SQL files a runner applies once each, in order, in transactions, and a file that ran is never edited.
- Values always travel as parameters, never inside the SQL text, and names like sort columns come from an allowlist in the code.
- The repository maps rows to domain types and turns no row into not found, which the service answers with a 404.
- Optional filters and keyset pages build the WHERE from fixed pieces, and ANY or a JOIN replaces N+1 queries.
- RETURNING gives back what a write stored, the row count tells whether it found the row, and SQLSTATEs map to 409 or 422.
